opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think when most people first hear about Deep Research, they picture the big, comprehensive report: you ask it to survey a market or summarize the literature on some topic, and it comes back with a long, structured document. That's genuinely useful, but the use case I keep coming back to is almost the opposite. It's finding that one obscure fact buried somewhere on the internet that you'd otherwise never track down.

Think about how you'd do that as a human. You'd search, click through ten links, realize none of them have it, rephrase your query, go to page three of the results, open some old forum thread or a PDF from a conference nobody remembers, and maybe after forty-five minutes you find it, or you give up. Most people give up. There's a whole class of questions people have basically stopped asking because the cost of finding the answer is too high.

What's interesting about Deep Research is that the model is really persistent in a way people aren't. It'll try dozens of different search strategies, read through pages that look irrelevant at first, notice a clue in one source that points it to another, and keep pulling that thread. That kind of needle-in-a-haystack browsing is exactly where a patient, tireless agent beats a person, because the bottleneck isn't intelligence so much as willingness to keep digging.

And I think it's underrated partly because it doesn't demo as flashily. A ten-page report looks impressive. A single sentence with the answer to your weird, specific question doesn't look like much. But if you've ever spent an afternoon trying to find, say, the exact spec of some discontinued part, or a quote someone supposedly said in a 2009 interview, you know how valuable it is to just get the answer, with a citation, in a few minutes. It unlocks curiosity you'd normally just let go.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research can find an obscure fact buried on the internet, including by following clues into old forum threads or obscure conference PDFs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when people talk about Deep Research, the thing that gets the most attention is these big, sprawling reports — you know, "give me a 20-page overview of the state of solid-state batteries" or whatever. And those are great, that's a real use case. But the thing I personally find myself coming back to more often is almost the opposite of that. It's the needle-in-a-haystack problem.

So the situation is something like: there's a fact that I'm pretty sure exists somewhere on the internet, but it's buried. It's in a GitHub issue from 2019, or it's in page four of some forum thread, or it's in a footnote of a paper that doesn't rank for any of the obvious search terms. And the way you'd find it as a human is you'd try a few queries, you'd read a bunch of stuff that's almost right but not quite, you'd pick up some new vocabulary from what you read, you'd refine the query, and you'd kind of iterate your way to it. That might take you 30 or 45 minutes, and a lot of the time you'd give up before you got there.

And that process — search, read, realize you were asking the wrong question, search again — is exactly what these agentic systems are good at. It's not one search. It's dozens of searches in sequence, where each one is informed by what came back from the last one. The model is persistent in a way that people usually aren't, because it doesn't get bored and it doesn't get frustrated.

I think the reason it's underrated is that the output isn't impressive-looking. You ask a question and you get back a sentence and a link. It doesn't feel like a big capability demo. But if you think about the actual value, a lot of the time that one fact is the thing that unblocks you — it's the config flag you needed, or the specific result from a paper that changes your plan, or the precedent that tells you someone's already tried the thing you were about to try. The report is nice to have; the rare fact is often the thing that actually mattered.

The other reason I like it is it's really easy to verify. With a long report, it's hard to know how much to trust it without basically redoing the work. With a single fact and a source, you click the link, you read the paragraph, and you're done. So it's a case where the model's strengths — persistence, breadth, tolerance for tedium — line up really well with a format where its weaknesses are easy to check.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research can find a fact buried online, giving examples such as an old GitHub issue, a forum thread, or a paper footnote.

astra-6.text:
I think we tend to focus on Deep Research as a way to produce a big report on a complicated topic. But there’s another really useful case where the answer you want might be a single sentence—it’s just incredibly hard to find.

With normal search, you’re doing a lot of that work yourself: trying different queries, opening pages, following clues, figuring out whether you’ve actually found the thing you were looking for. A research agent can take on that process. The value isn’t necessarily in how much it writes; it’s in how much searching it saves you.

The catch is that you need to check the source. For an obscure fact, a plausible answer isn’t enough. But if it can find the relevant evidence and point you to it, that’s a really powerful use case.

r001.rationale: The response describes finding an obscure fact that is incredibly hard to find through ordinary search, with the research agent searching pages and locating relevant evidence.

sol-6.1.text: I think people tend to think of Deep Research as a tool for producing a long report on a broad topic. But another really useful application is finding one very specific piece of information that’s buried somewhere on the internet. You might spend an hour trying different searches, following links, and checking whether you’ve actually found the right thing. Being able to delegate that search, and get back an answer with a source you can check, is incredibly valuable—even if the answer itself is just a sentence.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research can find a very specific piece of information buried somewhere on the internet, which clearly conveys locating obscure facts online.
